messages:
maya: hey team — running into a weird one with our streaming client + service account rotation. long story short: live stream will fail ~1m after start with a 401 and the response says 'invalid_token: aud mismatch'.

sanjay: ugh that sounds like the token being swapped for a different audience mid-stream. are you using id_tokens anywhere or only access tokens? :thinking:

maya: only access tokens (we call iamcredentials.generateAccessToken for the svcacct and attach as `Authorization: Bearer ...`)

leo: are you doing any token-exchange with STS or impersonation? sometimes the janitor job uses a different target_audience when minting and that creates an aud mismatch for the streaming endpoint.

maya: yes — we have a nightly janitor that proactively refreshes long-lived cached credentials. it calls the same generateAccessToken flow but with a small diff: it passes `audience: "sts-token"` in one branch. i thought audience only mattered for id_tokens?

rachel: audience matters for some token types. access tokens usually have an `aud` at issuance if minted via token-exchange. if your streaming service validates aud strictly, swapping in a token minted for a different audience will cause the 401.

leo: quick repro idea: start a stream, then run the janitor to rotate the token. does the stream socket stay open but server returns a 401 on next request? or does the socket drop immediately?

maya: socket stays open, next chunk attempt gets 401 + body: `{"error":"invalid_token","error_description":"aud mismatch: expected=redwood-inference got=sts-token"}`

sanjay: yep that matches. streaming server checks `aud` on every request. if your client swaps the header mid-stream the server rejects it.

rachel: two ways to fix: 1) make janitor mint tokens with the same audience your client uses (recommended), or 2) change client to detect aud mismatch and perform a silent reauth via the proper impersonation path. both are valid depending on constraints.

maya: for (2) — what's a pragmatic client pattern for streaming reconnect without losing state? we use Node client for stream, Rust backend for pipeline.

leo: pragmatic approach: keep a small refresh window and prefetch token before expiry (eg refresh when exp - now < 60s). attach a token-source function to the stream that always returns the current valid token. if you detect 401 + aud mismatch, close & reopen the stream with a fresh token from the correct flow and resume from last acked offset.

sanjay: sample Node pseudo:```js
// tokenProvider returns a Promise<string> with a valid access token
const token = await tokenProvider();
ws.send({type:'start', auth:`Bearer ${token}`});
// when 401/aud error arrives -> await tokenProvider(true) // force refresh
```

maya: thanks — our tokenProvider hits a cache that the janitor also writes to, so racey. maybe make the janitor update an opaque secret store and have provider read-only?

rachel: exactly. avoid multiple writers. janitor should rotate keys/credentials in a single atomic place (KMS-backed secret manager) and your clients should treat the secret store as read-only authority. write-only janitor pattern reduces races. :+1:

leo: also check if you're accidentally using id_tokens for downstream calls. id_tokens have `aud` that is whatever audience param you used when minting; they are not interchangeable with access tokens.

maya: quick followup: we noticed some languages (Rust client) were constructing `Authorization` header as `Bearer` + base64(jwt) when they should pass access token raw — introduced by a helper lib change. any red flags to look for across SDKs?

sanjay: common gotchas across SDKs: 1) sending id_token vs access_token, 2) accidentally double-encoding token, 3) using incorrect header name (Authorization vs authorization), 4) not adding a clock-skew buffer when checking `exp`.

rachel: if you want, paste the minimal header dump and i can eyeball it. also, we recently added a devex doc page about streaming auth gotchas with examples for Node/Rust — devex-bot will drop it.

devex-bot: heads-up: streaming auth guide -> https://internal.docs.redwood.ai/devex/streaming-auth-gotchas (node + rust examples, token rotation patterns, janitor best practices) :link:

maya: pasted header (sanitized):
```
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJI...
Content-Type: application/json
```

leo: that looks normal shape-wise. the token prefix is fine. validate the token locally with `jwt.io` or `openssl` to inspect `aud` and `exp`.

maya: did that — the `aud` flips after rotation (redwood-inference -> sts-token). so making janitor issue same audience will probably fix it.

sanjay: one more trick: if you can't change janitor, add a small compatibility layer in the streaming server that accepts the alternate audience but only from a trusted issuer and only if scoping matches (eg same project). that's a bit more risk but useful for graceful migration.

rachel: agree. audit logs + short-lived exception rule first. then lock it down after migration.

maya: thanks all — i'll switch janitor to use the proper target audience and change tokenProvider to refresh earlier. i'll follow up with a quick postmortem if this did the trick. :slightly_smiling_face:

leo: awesome — ping if you want a quick code review for the tokenProvider change.

maya: will do. :thumbsup:
